Land concentration, partially incorrect. Most of the pampean plain is owned by small farmers between 15 and 300 hectares. comments.author: @GBrunson
comments.text:
Milei’s economic formulas are brilliantly simple, I mean, if your goal is to make the government look richer while everyone else gets poorer.
Milei's formula to make the state have more money? Simple. Don’t pay the bills. None. Cut pensions, slash public spending, stop funding essential services, and let the government’s obligations pile up. Voilà, the books look better. It's like not paying your credit card bills at the end of the month, all of a sudden, you have more money.
Milei's formula to reduce inflation? Simple. Very simple. Take money out of people’s pockets. Cut purchasing power, squeeze wages, reduce consumption, and make ordinary people spend less because they simply can’t afford to. Voilà, inflation comes down. It’s the economic equivalent of saying, “We solved traffic jams by making everyone poor, so they had to sell their car."

Of course inflation can fall when demand collapses. But there’s a big difference between stabilizing an economy and making people poorer until they stop buying things.

Milei didn’t invent a miracle. He just took the most brutal version of austerity, wrapped it in libertarian rhetoric, and sold it as economic genius.

When people have less money, they buy less. When they buy less, prices have less pressure to rise. Congratulations, you’ve discovered the ancient economic principle of poverty as an anti inflation policy.

But after awhile the “magic” starts showing its tricks.

Because investors don’t put their money where the political slogans are. They put it where they believe they can get a good return.

For investors, ideology is one thing; making money is something completely different. Communist China and Vietnam are living proof of that. Investors don’t care nearly as much about political labels as politicians think they do. They care about stability, opportunity, risk, and, above all, return on investment.

And maybe that’s why the real test isn’t how loudly Milei praises libertarianism, Trump, or the free market. The real test is where international capital actually goes.

Brazil remains one of the world’s major destinations for foreign direct investment, ranking among the five largest recipients globally in 2025. And in the first half of 2026, center left Brazil attracted roughly US$49 billion in foreign investment, while libertarian, free market loving Argentina attracted only about US$1.5 billion.

In other words, investors put roughly 20 times more money into Brazil than into Argentina. So never mind the ideology.

Investors can listen to Milei’s speeches, watch the theatrics, applaud the libertarian revolution, and admire his political bromance with Trump. But when they actually open their wallets, they ask a much simpler question:

“Where is my money going to make money?”

That’s the difference between political ideology and investment reality.

And no amount of libertarian rhetoric, ideological wishful thinking, or political showmanship is going to change that calculation.

comments.author: @luffirton
comments.text:
Argentina’s Problem Isn’t Left vs Right — It’s Instability

Argentina doesn’t struggle because one side is “too protectionist” or the other is “too capitalist.”
It struggles because every election rewrites the entire economic model.
Populism swings back and forth, and long‑term planning becomes impossible.

This constant reset creates the same pattern every decade:
boom → bust → crisis → repeat.

If Argentina wants real stability, it needs one part of the economy that politics can’t tear down every four years.

That’s where Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) come in.

Think of them as islands of stability:

• Long‑term rules
• Predictable regulations
• Free‑trade orientation
• Protection from sudden policy changes
• A legal framework built for foreign investment


This is basically how Shenzhen kick‑started China’s industrial rise.

EEZs would let Argentina grow export‑oriented industries without being dragged into the protectionism vs. liberalization tug‑of‑war every time commodity prices move.

Over time, these zones could:

• Diversify the economy beyond agriculture
• Attract long‑term industrial investment
• Strengthen the currency
• Reduce vulnerability to global price swings


Argentina doesn’t need to pick one ideology forever.
It needs a dual‑track system:
Stable EEZs + flexible national policy.

Predictability is the missing ingredient — and the key to breaking the boom‑and‑bust cycle.

comments.author: @hectordenicola
comments.text:
Hi. I'm from Uruguay. I think this is a very interesting video. The distribution of land is quite an issue in Argentina. I would have liked a comparison with the USA cause there they had the Homestead act that probably made a huge difference in terms of how land was distributed. That said, I'd like to mention that a couple great historians of Argentina's economy, Pablo Gerchunoff and Lucas LLach, have come up with another explanation (which is not at odds with yours): Argentina's population has a level of economic demands that can't be met by it's low productivity. What they mean is that it is a society that got to be rich by the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th. This was possible because they exported their goods to England at high prices. Once this was no longer possible they got poor but their population would not accept it, so politicians had to keep coming up with the populism card promising that they would bring Argentina back to its feet. And since they had no clue of how to achieve this they would just grow the national debt or print money in a neverending cycle. 
At a lower intensity, I think this is the same thing that happens to Uruguay. We shared the same richness at the beginning of the 20th century and now we don't have the productivity to keep the welfare state we had in the past. Fortunately our politicians are not even nearly as deranged as those from Argentina, but we are in a collision course anyway, just at a slower pace. Not even the right wing politicias would dare to say that we have to cut spending cause we can't afford it.

replies.author: @hectordenicola
replies.text: @GeographyEffect Well, although I'm not a big fan of Peronism, I have to be fair with it. They did exacerbate Argentina's populism, but as far as I know from many economics historians the downfall started in the 30s when England, after the crisis of 1929, decided not to buy anymore meat from abroad other than from its own colonies or former colonies. Argentina had to negotiate and signed a treaty which is infamous from the left wing standpoint: the Roca-Runciman treaty. Of course, this left Argentina in a worse situation than the favourable conditions the previously had. But being more reasonable, on e could argue: What else could they do? In the end I think that the whole thing boils down to the fact that Argentina was never actually developed. They mainly produced raw materials and they totally depended on their prices. Same thing happend to Uruguay. Fortunatelly we never went into the populism spiral, but I think that it is very likely that we will reach that point

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s a very interesting complement to the geographic argument. A society can inherit expectations from an earlier era of unusually high income, and if productivity later falls short of those expectations, the political system can end up repeatedly financing the gap through debt, inflation, or redistribution.

comments.author: @KeithBarnesLife
comments.text: This is a great video, but there's an angle that could have made it even better - the main argument of the video (centralization of resources and the resource curse) is on the cusp of breaking due to significant oil & natural gas in Tierra del Fuego, and one of the world's largest lithium reserves in the northwest. The video could have set out the opportunity for the Canada-/Australia-esque distribution of political power as the economy diversifies into broader exports while, at the same time, it could have shown how the capital to invest in the extraction and exportation of these resources could depend on the profit of agricultural exports - hinting to an opportunity like that of the early 2000s that could yet be lost again if the vested interests you explained continue to get their way.

comments.author: @fcuneo1971
comments.text:
If anything, the Pampas is a blessing, we are lucky to have them.
The only problem with it comes if you over rely on one sector for your exports. Argentina being a developing country needs to earn their foreign currency in order to pay for imports.

The problem here is the over reliance on a sector that is highly volatile, not only is dependent on the export prices for the commodities, but we are also weather dependent. If it rains great, but when it doesn’t then harvests get smaller and worse quality, there is less money coming in, less taxes and less dollars, next thing people have learned over the years is that a financial crisis is around the corner, so they try to anticipate it and they end up generating one 😢

Good thing is that now the country is diversifying with oil and gas from Vaca Muerta and Milei government has opened the door also to huge mining projects so we should not depend  in the future not so much on farming for our economy

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s a strong way to frame it. The Pampas are clearly an advantage, but dependence on a volatile export base creates recurring vulnerability; Vaca Muerta and mining could matter most if they genuinely broaden the sources of foreign exchange rather than simply replacing one concentrated resource sector with another.
